scenes.summary: Chao Pulai disputes the succession of his half-brother Sukhrangphaa and conspires with maternal Kamata envoys for military support.

scenes.summary: Rather than shedding fraternal blood, Sukhrangphaa welcomes Chao Pulai back into the court and effects complete reconciliation.

scenes.title: Appointment of Chao Pulai as Governor of Sadiya
scenes.summary: King Sukhrangphaa invests Chao Pulai with governorship of the critical eastern frontier outpost of Sadiya.

scenes.title: Nangchukham Borgohain Marches on Kamata
scenes.summary: Tai Sulai flees to Kamata. Sudangphaa's commander Nangchukham Borgohain invades, and the Kamata king, also pressed by Bengal, makes peace and gives a daughter in marriage to Sudangphaa.

scenes.summary: Forewarned by his courageous wife Joymoti, tall and muscular Prince Gadapani flees in disguise into the Naga hills to evade royal executioners.

scenes.title: Martyrdom of Princess Joymoti Konwari
scenes.summary: Tied to thorn bushes on Jerenga Pathar and brutally tortured for 14 continuous days by Lora Raja's agents, Princess Joymoti breathes her last refusing to betray her husband Gadapani.

characters.name: Phuleswari (Pramatheswari)
characters.role: Queen who ruled as Bar Raja
characters.summary: A dancer of the Nat caste made Bar Raja under Siva Singha after astrologers predicted the king's fall. Minted coins in joint names and pressed to make Shaktism the state religion; died in 1731 in childbirth.
characters.notes: Her insult to the Moamoria Gosains is cited as a cause of the later rebellion.

scenes.title: Transfer of Royal Power to Queen Phuleswari (Bar Raja)
scenes.summary: Panicked by astrological predictions of Chhatra-bhanga (loss of kingship), Siva Singha transfers the sovereign umbrella, royal seal, and rule to his chief queen Phuleswari.

scenes.title: Excavation of Gaurisagar Tank and Temples
scenes.summary: Queen Phuleswari excavates Gaurisagar tank and erects temples dedicated to Shiva, Vishnu, and Devi along its banks.

scenes.title: Queen Phuleswari's Persecution of Moamoria Vaishnavas
scenes.summary: Queen Phuleswari aggressively enforces Shakta worship, compelling Moamoria Vaishnavite Mahantas to smear sacrificial animal blood on their foreheads, igniting decades of bitter hatred.

characters.name: Ambika

scenes.title: Construction of Sivasagar Tank (Bor Pukhuri) and Shiva Dol
scenes.summary: Queen Ambika excavates the monumental 257-acre Sivasagar tank and erects the 104-foot-high Shiva Dol, one of India's tallest stone temple shikhara towers.

scenes.title: Painting of the Hastividyarnava
scenes.summary: Under Siva Singha and Queen Ambika, Sukumar Barkaith writes the Hastividyarnava, a treatise on royal elephants, illustrated by the painters Dilbar and Dosai.

scenes.title: A Bhuyan Boyhood at Alipukhuri
scenes.summary: The orphaned boy Sankara (later Sankardev), raised by his grandmother Khersuti in a chief Baro-Bhuyan family near Bordowa, starts school under Mahendra Kandali at about age 12.

scenes.title: Sankardev Stages the Chihna Yatra
scenes.summary: Young Sankardev stages a dance-drama, the Chihna Yatra, the first of the plays and performances that grow into Ankiya Naat and the satra theatre tradition.

scenes.title: Madhavdev Meets Sankardev
scenes.summary: At Dhuwahat, after a long debate, Madhavdev accepts Sankardev as his guru and becomes his chief disciple.

scenes.title: Execution of Hari and Sankardeva Leaves the Ahom Kingdom
scenes.summary: Under Suklenmung, Hari, the son-in-law of the Vaishnava saint Sankardeva, is captured and executed. Sankardeva leaves the Ahom kingdom for Koch territory.

scenes.title: The Prayer House at Patbausi
scenes.summary: Settled at Patbausi near Barpeta in Koch territory, Sankardev gathers disciples around a prayer house, the pattern of the namghar and the satra.

scenes.title: Weaving the Vrindavani Vastra
scenes.summary: For Nara Narayan, master weavers at Tantikuchi near Barpeta, guided by Sankardev, weave a long silk cloth showing Krishna’s life in Vrindavan.

scenes.title: Sankardev Answers the Pundits
scenes.summary: Accused of spreading a new faith, Sankardev goes into hiding when Nara Narayan orders his arrest. Brought to court through Chilarai, he answers the pundits in debate; the king frees him and seats him near the throne.

scenes.title: Sankardev’s Last Days at Bheladonga
scenes.summary: Sankardev dies at Bheladonga near the Koch capital, having declined Nara Narayan’s request to become his disciple.

scenes.title: Mahapurusha Srimanta Sankardev
scenes.summary: 15th–16th century saint-scholar, polymath, playwright, social reformer, and founder of Ekasarana Dharma and the Sattriya cultural tradition.

scenes.title: Srimanta Sankardev Writing on Sanchi-Pat
scenes.summary: Depiction of Guru Sankardev composing hymns, Kirtana Ghosha, and Ankiya Nat dramas on bark manuscripts (Sanchi-pat).

scenes.title: Srimanta Sankardev in Contemplation
scenes.summary: Contemplative and serene spiritual portrayal of Mahapurusha Srimanta Sankardev radiating spiritual wisdom.

scenes.title: Mahapurusha Sankardev Preaching Bhakti
scenes.summary: Srimanta Sankardev expounding the universal humanist message of devotion, equality, and compassion to disciples.

scenes_without_characters.title: Carving the Temples of Madan Kamdev
scenes_without_characters.summary: Masons and sculptors raise stone temples at Madan Kamdev, near Baihata Chariali, carving Uma-Maheshvara embracing, the Sun, Ganesha, Vidyadharas, apsaras and animals.

scenes_without_characters.title: A Regional Chief Hears Local Petitions
scenes_without_characters.summary: After the fall of the Kamarupa Palas the valley splits into small domains. A local chief hears petitions at his timber court.

scenes_without_characters.title: A Village Sustains the Feeding House
scenes_without_characters.summary: In one of the seven endowed villages, farmers bring in the harvest that will feed Vallabhadeva’s feeding house.

scenes_without_characters.title: River Trade Between Regional Centres
scenes_without_characters.summary: Boats unload goods at a river landing between the small kingdoms of the valley.

scenes_without_characters.title: First Ministerial Interregnum
scenes_without_characters.summary: Following Sutuphaa's treacherous assassination, the Burhagohain and Borgohain rule jointly for four years due to the absence of an acceptable adult royal prince.

scenes_without_characters.title: Second Ministerial Interregnum
scenes_without_characters.summary: Ministers Burhagohain and Borgohain hold executive power for eight years following the assassination of Tyao Khamti while searching for the exiled royal prince.

scenes_without_characters.title: Smiths and Salt Wells of Sadiya
scenes_without_characters.summary: Chutia blacksmiths, bell-metal workers and goldsmiths, and the salt springs at Borhat, make the kingdom one of the most productive of the valley.

scenes_without_characters.title: The Chutia Regalia Carried Away
scenes_without_characters.summary: After the rout at the Dibru fort and the death of the Chutia king, the Ahoms carry off the royal heirlooms: the gold and silver cat (mekuri), the royal umbrella and the bedstead.

scenes_without_characters.title: Artisans Taken to the Ahom Capital
scenes_without_characters.summary: Brahmans, Kayasthas and artisans are moved from Sadiya to the Ahom capital; one account says some 3,000 blacksmiths were settled at Bosa and Ujoni. Chutia cannons and hand-guns (hiloi) pass to the Ahoms.

scenes_without_characters.title: A New Capital at Maibong
scenes_without_characters.summary: After a 22-year interregnum following the loss of Dimapur, Nirbhaya Narayana sets up the Dimasa capital at Maibong in the hills.

scenes_without_characters.title: The Koch Fleet Routed
scenes_without_characters.summary: Rebuilt after the Treaty of Majuli, Ahom forces rout the Koch river fleet under Tepu Barua.

scenes_without_characters.title: Turned Back at the Dhansiri
scenes_without_characters.summary: The last Koch expedition against the Ahoms is repulsed at the Dhansiri.

scenes_without_characters.title: The Mughal Fleet Sails from Dhaka
scenes_without_characters.summary: Allied with Lakshmi Narayan of Koch Bihar, the Mughal governor of Bengal sends an army and a river fleet from near Dhaka against Koch Hajo. By the end of the year the kingdom is occupied.

scenes_without_characters.title: The Court Moves to Khaspur
scenes_without_characters.summary: Koch rule at Khaspur in the Barak valley ends, the state merges with the Dimasa kingdom, and Khaspur becomes the Dimasa capital.

scenes_without_characters.title: Manipur under Burmese Occupation
scenes_without_characters.summary: Burmese armies occupy Manipur, and many Manipuris flee to Cachar and Sylhet.

scenes_without_characters.title: Gomdhar Konwar's Revolt
scenes_without_characters.summary: Former Ahom nobles led by Dhananjoy Borgohain crown the prince Gomdhar Konwar near Jorhat and march on Rangpur. Lieutenant Rutherford's troops defeat them; Gomdhar is captured and banished. The first armed rising against British rule in Assam.

scenes_without_characters.title: The Jaintia Kingdom Annexed

scenes_without_characters.title: Phulaguri Dhewa
scenes_without_characters.summary: Peasants at Phulaguri in Nagaon rise against new taxes; police fire on the gathering, and leaders are hanged or deported.

scenes_without_characters.title: Assamese Restored in Schools and Courts
scenes_without_characters.summary: After decades of Bengali as the official language, Assamese is restored in the schools and courts of Assam, a campaign begun by Anandaram Dhekial Phukan and the missionaries.

scenes_without_characters.title: Assam Becomes a Province
scenes_without_characters.summary: Assam is separated from Bengal as a Chief Commissioner’s province, with Sylhet and the hill districts.

scenes_without_characters.title: Patharughat
scenes_without_characters.summary: At Patharughat in Darrang, troops fire on peasants gathered to protest a steep rise in land revenue.

scenes_without_characters.title: Eastern Bengal and Assam

scenes_without_characters.title: Gandhi in Assam
scenes_without_characters.summary: Gandhi tours Assam during the Non-Cooperation movement; foreign cloth is burnt and Assamese join the national movement in numbers.

scenes_without_characters.title: The Sylhet Referendum
scenes_without_characters.summary: Sylhet votes to join East Pakistan, and Assam enters independence without it.

scenes_without_characters.title: The Great Earthquake

scenes_without_characters.title: War Reaches Bomdila
scenes_without_characters.summary: In the Sino-Indian war, Chinese forces take Bomdila; Tezpur is evacuated before the ceasefire.

realms.name: Kamarupa: the traditional bounds
realms.summary: The bounds that later texts give for Kamarupa, from the Karatoya in the west to the far east, with the Brahmaputra's course near Mymensingh in the south and Kanchenjunga in the north.
realms.boundary: West: Karatoya river | East: Sadiya (the Kalika Purana also gives Lalitakanta near Guwahati; Dikkaravasini, linked to the Dikrong river, and Dikshu, linked to the Dibang) | South: the Brahmaputra's junction near the Dhaka and Mymensingh districts | North: Kanchenjunga
realms.notes: Textual, not period-specific: the sources are Xuanzang (7th c.), the Kalika Purana (10th c.) and the Yogini Tantra (16th c.). No inscription confirms these bounds, and Shin (2018) calls it futile to project any fixed boundary on Kamarupa, which never formed a single entity.

realms.name: Kamarupa under the Varmans: reach, not a boundary
realms.summary: The Varman kings pushed outward: Kalyanavarman took Davaka (the Kopili valley), Mahendravarman extended control eastward, Sylhet (the Chandrapuri visaya) was held by the time of the Nidhanpur grant, and Sthitavarman and Bhaskaravarman campaigned against Gauda at Karnasuvarna.
realms.boundary: West: no river named for this period (tradition gives the Karatoya) | East: 'further eastern areas' (no river named) | South-west: Sylhet and the Gauda frontier at Karnasuvarna
realms.notes: The sources read give conquests and findspots, not river boundaries. Pundravardhana is named as Xuanzang's starting point, not as a conquest.

realms.name: Kamarupa under the Palas
realms.summary: A core on the south bank of the Brahmaputra around Kamarupanagara; the western territories were lost to Ramapala of Bengal, and local chiefs held parts of Kamrup, Darrang and Sonitpur on the north bank.
realms.boundary: Core: the south bank of the Brahmaputra | West: lost to Ramapala of Bengal (no river named) | North bank: held by local rulers such as Bhaskara in Kamrup, Darrang and Sonitpur
realms.notes: The article read states these extents without naming rivers beyond the Brahmaputra; the Pala chronology is unsettled.

realms.name: Kamata, c. 1257 to 1440
realms.summary: The kingdom of Sandhya and his successors: from the Karatoya in the west to the Barnadi in the east, including Rangpur and northern Mymensingh to the south. Control east of the Manas was loose.
realms.boundary: West: Karatoya river | East: Barnadi river (control beyond the Manas 'lax') | North: the Bhutan hills | South: Rangpur and northern Mymensingh
realms.notes: Reconstructed from epigraphy and later tradition. The north and south limits are as listed in the source (Kamrup, Goalpara, Jalpaiguri, Cooch Behar, Rangpur and northern Mymensingh), not river lines.

realms.name: The Khen kingdom of Kamata
realms.summary: Niladhwaj, Chakradhwaj and Nilambar ruled from Kamatapur between the Karatoya and the Barnadi.
realms.boundary: West: Karatoya river | East: Barnadi river | Capital: Kamatapur (Gosanimari)
realms.notes: The span is from Sarkar. A claim that Nilambar widened the kingdom into parts of West Bengal, Mymensingh and Dinajpur is uncited.

realms.name: Husain Shah's Kamata (the Sultanate's reach)
realms.summary: After taking Kamatapur, Alauddin Husain Shah held the region to Hajo by 1502; one account pushes it east to the Barnadi by defeating Harup Narayan. The Bhuyans then destroyed Danyal's garrison.
realms.boundary: West: Karatoya river | East: Hajo (by 1502); the Barnadi in one account (the Baro-Bhuyan article)
realms.notes: The two eastern limits come from different sources.

realms.name: The early Koch kingdom of Biswa Singha
realms.summary: Biswa Singha's kingdom ran from the Karatoya in the west to the Barnadi in the east.
realms.boundary: West: Karatoya river | East: Barnadi river | South: Ghoraghat (Rangpur) in one study
realms.notes: Another account describes a late Koch-Kamata extent from the Teesta to the Sankosh instead; the dates and sources differ.

realms.name: Nara Narayan's undivided Koch kingdom
realms.summary: At its widest the undivided Koch kingdom reached far east: from the Karatoya (or the Sankosh) in the west to the Bhareli (Kameng), and briefly the Subansiri, in the east.
realms.boundary: West: Karatoya river (the Kamrup article) or Sankosh river (the Koch Hajo article) | East: Bhareli (Kameng) river; the Subansiri briefly (via the Treaty of Majuli), after which the Ahoms pushed Koch control back to the Bhareli
realms.notes: The sources give competing descriptions. Kamata's control beyond the Manas had always been lax.

realms.name: Koch Hajo
realms.summary: The eastern half of Nara Narayan's divided kingdom, on the north bank of the Brahmaputra from the Sankosh to the Bhareli, with land south of the river west of the Kolong-Kopili.
realms.boundary: West: Sankosh river (the border with Koch Bihar) | East: Bhareli (Bharali) river | South: west of the Kalang-Kopili river, to the forests of Mymensingh
realms.notes: A mirrored older text names the Subansiri as the dividing line instead of the Sankosh; the main source says Sankosh.

realms.name: Koch Bihar
realms.summary: The western half of the divided kingdom, west of the Sankosh, the line that is roughly today's Assam-West Bengal border.
realms.boundary: East: Sankosh river | West: the Koch Bihar lands towards the Teesta and Karatoya
realms.notes: Only the Sankosh boundary is given in the sources read.

realms.name: Mughal Kamrup
realms.summary: The Mughal sarkars on the Koch Hajo lands: Dhekeri between the Sankosh and the Manas, and Kamrup between the Manas and the Barnadi. By 1615 the Mughal frontier reached the Barnadi.
realms.boundary: Dhekeri: between the Sankosh and Manas rivers | Kamrup: between the Manas and Barnadi rivers | East limit by 1615: Barnadi river
realms.notes: Largely congruent with the British Kamrup district of 1833-36. Wade (1805) gives Kamrup as bounded by the Manas (west), Raotan (north), Barnadi (east) and Brahmaputra (south).

realms.name: The Treaty of Asurar Ali boundary
realms.summary: After the Mughal-Ahom war, the Barnadi on the north bank and Asurar Ali on the south bank marked the limit; the Ahom king recognised Mughal supremacy in Kamrup and the Mughals held western Assam from Guwahati to the Manas.
realms.boundary: North bank: Barnadi river | South bank: Asurar Ali (a causeway at Guwahati, believed to be Rajgarh Road); the Ahom-Mughal conflicts article gives the Kalang instead
realms.notes: The two Wikipedia articles disagree on the southern mark (Asurar Ali vs Kalang). Mir Jumla's advance in 1662 was measured against this line.

realms.name: The Treaty of Ghilajharighat boundary
realms.summary: After Mir Jumla took Garhgaon, the Ahoms ceded Guwahati's side of the valley: on the north bank Guwahati to Samdhara on the Bharali, on the south bank Guwahati to the Kolong, and the Manas-to-Guwahati region was returned to the Mughals.
realms.boundary: North bank: Guwahati to Samdhara on the Bharali river | South bank: Guwahati to the Kolong river | Also: the region between the Manas and Guwahati returned to the Mughals
realms.notes: The infobox places the signing at Panibat of Tipam on the Dihing; the article does not say where Ghilajharighat is. The Barnadi does not appear in the 1663 terms.

realms.name: The early Ahom kingdom
realms.summary: Settlements on both banks of the Brahmaputra and on Majuli, around Charaideo; the Dikhow marked the frontier with the Kacharis from the 1270s. In the Buranji division of the early offices, the Burhagohain's land lay between Sadiya and the Gerelua on the north bank and the Borgohain's west to the Burai.
realms.boundary: East: the Patkai hills | West: Dikhow river (the Ahom-Kachari frontier) | Offices: Burhagohain between Sadiya and the Gerelua river (north bank); Borgohain to the west up to the Burai river
realms.notes: The Dikhow frontier is in the project's own scenes (AHOM-026 to 031); the Gerelua and Burai limits are from the Ahom kingdom article, and neither river is placed here.

realms.name: The Ahom kingdom after the Chutia annexation
realms.summary: The annexation added Sadiya, Habung, Dihing (Mungklang) and the Kaliabor side; land west of the Dhansiri came from the Kacharis, and by 1536 Ahom rule reached the Kolong in Nagaon.
realms.boundary: East: Sadiya | West: the Dhansiri (from c. 1526), then the Kolong river in Nagaon (by 1536)
realms.notes: The article gives both 1523 and 1524 for the Chutia annexation, and does not name a river for the western edge in 1523.

realms.name: The Ahom kingdom at its greatest extent
realms.summary: Under Jayadhwaj Singha the Ahoms occupied Kamrup and held the Brahmaputra valley from Sadiya in the east, the greatest extent; Mir Jumla took Garhgaon in 1662 and the Kamrup gains were lost.
realms.boundary: East: Sadiya | West: Kamrup (no river named in the source)
realms.notes: The article gives no western river for this peak.

realms.name: The Ahom kingdom from 1682: the Manas frontier
realms.summary: After the Battle of Itakhuli the Manas became the western boundary of the Ahom kingdom and stayed so until the British; the Borphukan ruled from Guwahati over the land from the Manas to Kaliabor, and Kamrup then matched the later British district.
realms.boundary: West: Manas river | East: Sadiya and the Patkai | Borphukan's domain: the Manas to Kaliabor
realms.notes: Itakhuli is dated August 1682 in most sources (the project's scenes date its recapture to 1667). Kamrup's eastern edge is the Barnadi in the Mughal and British accounts.

realms.name: The Chutia kingdom
realms.summary: A kingdom of the north-bank valleys of the Subansiri, Brahmaputra, Lohit and Dihing, with Sadiya as its seat; one study gives it from the Sisi in the west to the Brahmaputra in the east with the hills to the north and the Buri Dihing to the south. Its influence may have reached Biswanath in Darrang.
realms.boundary: West: Sisi river | East: the Brahmaputra, and on the north bank Parshuram Kund | North: the hills | South: Buri Dihing | Heartland: the Subansiri, Brahmaputra, Lohit and Dihing valleys
realms.notes: The source's own wording is odd (Sisi west to the Brahmaputra east); the Ahom border is not defined by a river in the article (a 1513 conflict led to Dikhowmukh). Kings' lists are unreliable.

realms.name: The early Dimasa (Kachari) kingdom
realms.summary: Dimasa power lay from the Dikhow in the east to the Kolong in the west, including the Dhansiri valley and the North Cachar hills; one Dimasa tradition puts the eastern limit at the Mohong or Namdang. The Ahom Buranji instead describes the kingdom from the Kopili to the Dhansiri. Capital: Dimapur until 1536, then Maibong.
realms.boundary: East: Dikhow river (Ahom account); the Mohong or Namdang (Dimasa tradition) | West: Kolong river, or the Kopili in the Ahom Buranji | Core: the Dhansiri valley and the North Cachar hills
realms.notes: Mostly popular and community sources; the Kolong-Kopili and Dhansiri differences are contested.

realms.name: The Dimasa kingdom in the 17th century
realms.summary: By the reign of Birdarpan Narayan the Kacharis had withdrawn from the Dhansiri valley, which reverted to jungle and became a barrier between their kingdom and the Ahoms.
realms.boundary: North and east: the Dhansiri valley left as a jungle buffer | Capital: Maibong
realms.notes: One summary of a community source.

places.name: Barnadi

places.name: Teesta

places.name: Dikhou

places.name: Dihing

places.name: Namdang

places.name: Davaka

places.name: Charagua
places.location: On the Dihing river, Upper Assam (exact place not established)
places.summary: A later Ahom capital built on the Dihing.
places.notes: Present-day place not established in the sources read.

places.name: Garhgaon
places.summary: An Ahom capital from the 17th century, with the Kareng Ghar palace.
places.notes: District placement not re-checked.

places.name: Kareng Ghar
places.summary: The seven-storey palace of the Ahom kings at Garhgaon, rebuilt in brick in the 18th century.

places.name: Sivasagar
places.summary: The Ahom capital Rangpur (1699 to 1788), renamed for the Sivasagar tank dug in 1733.
places.notes: In Ahom scenes 'Rangpur' means this town. Kamata texts also mention Rangpur in present Bangladesh; see rangpur-bangladesh.

places.name: Rang Ghar
places.summary: The royal sports pavilion of the Ahom kings, an early 18th-century amphitheatre.

places.name: Joysagar
places.summary: The great tank dug by Rudra Singha in memory of his mother Joymoti, with temples on its bank.

places.name: Jorhat
places.summary: The last Ahom capital (from 1794), and the site of Lachit's maidam at Hoolungapara.

places.name: Hoolungapara
places.summary: Site of the Lachit Maidam built by Udayaditya Singha.

places.name: Mahgarh
places.summary: Where Chandrakanta Singha camped and lost to the Burmese in April 1822.
places.notes: Location given in the project's scene text.

places.name: Majuli
places.summary: The great river island of the Brahmaputra, a centre of Vaishnava satras.

places.name: Sadiya
places.summary: The seat of the Chutia kingdom, taken by the Ahoms in 1523-24.

places.name: Bengmara
places.summary: The seat of the Moran and Matak chiefs during the Moamoria rebellions.
places.notes: Identification with the Tinsukia area is approximate.

places.name: Saraighat
places.location: Guwahati, Assam (the narrowest reach of the Brahmaputra)
places.summary: Site of the great naval battle of March 1671.

places.name: Itakhuli
places.location: South bank of the Brahmaputra near Nilachal, Guwahati, Assam
places.summary: The Mughal garrison fort retaken by the Ahoms (1667 in the project's scenes; August 1682 in other sources).
places.notes: The date differs between sources; one gives the fort's site as the present Deputy Commissioner's bungalow.

places.name: Alaboi
places.location: Near Dalbari, Assam (exact present place not established)
places.summary: Site of the 1669 defeat in which about 10,000 Ahom soldiers died.
places.notes: The sources read give only 'Alaboi plains' and 'Alaboi hills near Dalbari'.

places.name: Kaliabor
places.summary: The seat of the Borphukan; Lachit died here in April 1672.

places.name: Kajali
places.summary: The first seat of the Borphukan and the Ahom outpost at the mouth of the Kolong; first Mughal foray in 1615.
places.notes: Exact site approximate.

places.name: Samdhara
places.present_name: On the Bharali (Kameng) river, north bank (per the 1663 treaty text)
places.summary: Ahom fort where the Mughal fleet was destroyed in a night attack.
places.notes: The Treaty of Ghilajharighat text places Samdhara on the Bharali river; the AHOM map point sits near Tezpur, which agrees. Another source mentions a Samdhara fort resisting the Mughals around 1636.

places.name: Duimunisila
places.summary: Place of the naval fight that stopped the Mughal advance in the early Mughal war.
places.notes: Present-day place not established in the sources read.

places.name: Ghilajharighat
places.summary: Where the Treaty of Ghilajharighat of January 1663 was signed after Mir Jumla's invasion.
places.notes: Present-day place not established in the sources read.

places.name: Dhubri
places.summary: A frontier town on the lower Brahmaputra, the western limit of Ahom control at times.

places.name: Nagaon
places.summary: A central Assam town and district, where Iwaz Khalji's army was turned back in 1226-27 (per the Gachtal inscription).

places.name: Dimapur
places.summary: The Dimasa (Kachari) capital until the 16th century, with brick walls, tanks and carved pillars.

places.name: Maibong
places.summary: The Dimasa capital after Dimapur was abandoned.

places.name: Kamatapur
places.summary: The capital of Kamata from about 1257, and of the Khen kings; destroyed in 1498.
places.notes: Sources place it near Cooch Behar or at Gosanimari.

places.name: Cooch Behar
places.summary: The Koch Bihar capital in the 16th century, near the old Kamatapur.

places.name: Gachtal
places.summary: Findspot of an inscription of the Sultanate wars; where allies fought Sikandar Shah in 1362.
places.notes: Standard identification as given in the sources read.

places.name: Langamaguri
places.location: North of Guwahati, Assam (exact place not established)
places.summary: Where Chandivara's group of Kayastha and Brahmin families were settled by Kamata's kings.

places.name: Bordowa
places.summary: The village of Sankardev's birth and early life, in the Bhuyan country.
places.notes: His birthplace is also given as Patekibari near Bhuragaon.

places.name: Hajo
places.summary: The limit of Husain Shah's conquest by 1502; later a Koch seat.

places.name: Rangpur (Bangladesh)
places.summary: Held by Dharmanarayan after the split of Kamata; not the Ahom Rangpur (Sivasagar).

places.name: Gaur
places.location: Malda district, West Bengal, on the Bangladesh border
places.summary: The capital of the Bengal Sultanate and earlier Gauda.
places.notes: Lakhnauti was the Sultanate's regional centre near Gaur.

places.name: Devkot
places.summary: The Bengal Sultanate's frontier base from which Bakhtiyar Khalji set out in 1206.

places.name: Sonargaon
places.summary: The eastern Bengal capital from which Bahadur Shah raided Kamata in 1321-22.

places.name: Sylhet
places.summary: A region held by rulers claiming Kamarupa's legacy.

places.name: Kanauj
places.summary: Harsha's capital, where the great assembly of c. 643 was held.

places.name: Thanesar
places.summary: The early seat of Harsha's family.

places.name: Nalanda
places.summary: The Buddhist monastic university where Xuanzang studied.

places.name: Allahabad Pillar
places.summary: Samudragupta's pillar inscription, the first written mention of Kamarupa.

places.name: Aphsad
places.summary: Findspot of Adityasena's inscription, which records Mahasenagupta's defeat of Susthitavarman.
places.notes: District not re-checked.

places.name: Malwa
places.summary: A Gupta-period kingdom whose raid on Kamarupa is noted in the Varman story.

places.name: Delhi
places.summary: The seat of the Sultanate and then the Mughal court.

places.name: Kamauli
places.summary: Findspot of Vaidyadeva's copper-plate grant.
places.notes: Standard identification; not re-checked here.

places.name: Ava
places.summary: The Burmese capital area that sent armies into Assam in 1817-1826.

places.name: Yandabo
places.summary: Where the Treaty of Yandabo (1826) ended the First Anglo-Burmese War and Burmese rule in Assam.

places.name: Dikhowmukh
places.location: At the mouth of the Dikhow river, Sivasagar district, Assam (approximate)
places.summary: Where the Dikhow river meets the Brahmaputra.
places.notes: From the catalogue coordinates; not otherwise checked.

places.name: Singri
places.location: Darrang district, Assam (approximate, from the coordinates)
places.summary: A place on the Ahom map catalogue.
places.notes: Identified only from the catalogue coordinates; not otherwise checked.

places.name: Narayanpur
places.summary: A place on the Ahom map catalogue.
places.notes: Identified only from the catalogue coordinates; not otherwise checked.

places.name: Biswanath
places.summary: A town on the north bank of the Brahmaputra.

places.name: Dergaon
places.summary: A town in Upper Assam.

places.name: Auniati Satra
places.summary: A Vaishnava satra on Majuli.

places.name: Jogighopa
places.summary: A town on the Brahmaputra in Lower Assam.

places.name: Jerenga Pathar
places.summary: The field near Sivasagar associated with Joymoti.
places.notes: Location as given in the AHOM catalogue.

places.name: Umananda
places.location: Peacock Island in the Brahmaputra, Guwahati, Assam
places.summary: A Shiva temple on Peacock Island at Guwahati.

places.name: Jaintiapur
places.summary: The capital of the Jaintia kingdom.
places.notes: Present-day location from standard references; not re-checked.

places.name: Siva Dol
places.location: Bank of the Sivasagar tank, Sivasagar, Assam
places.summary: The great Shiva temple on the Sivasagar tank.

places.name: Talatal Ghar
places.summary: The Ahom palace with underground levels.

places.name: Manipur
places.summary: The hill kingdom south of Assam.

places.name: Nazira
places.summary: A town near Garhgaon.

places.name: Dibrugarh
places.summary: A city on the Brahmaputra in Upper Assam.

places.name: Tinsukia
places.summary: A town and district in the far east of Upper Assam.

places.name: Ledo
places.summary: A town at the foot of the Patkai range.

places.name: Golaghat
places.summary: A town and district in Upper Assam.

places.name: North Lakhimpur
places.summary: A town on the north bank in Upper Assam.

places.name: Barpeta
places.summary: A town in Lower Assam.

places.name: Goalpara
places.summary: A town on the Brahmaputra in western Assam.

places.name: Mayong
places.summary: A village known in Assamese lore for magic.

places.name: Kaziranga
places.summary: A great wetland and grassland reserve south of the Brahmaputra.

places.name: Kohima
places.summary: The capital of Nagaland, in the Naga hills.

places.name: Imphal
places.summary: The capital of Manipur.

places.name: Silchar
places.summary: The main city of the Barak valley.

places.name: Bhamo
places.summary: A river town on the Irrawaddy near the old Tai routes.

places.name: Tawang
places.summary: A Buddhist centre in the western Himalaya.

places.name: Hukawng Valley
places.summary: The valley traditionally linked to the Tai homeland.

places.name: Hayagriva Madhava Temple
places.summary: A temple at Hajo, sacred to Hindus and Buddhists.

places.name: Dakhinpat Satra
places.summary: A Vaishnava satra on Majuli.

places.name: Kamalabari Satra
places.summary: A Vaishnava satra on Majuli.

places.name: Garamur Satra
places.summary: A Vaishnava satra on Majuli.

places.name: Barpeta Satra
places.summary: The Vaishnava satra at Barpeta.

places.name: Pandu
places.summary: A port quarter of Guwahati on the south bank of the Brahmaputra.

places.name: Mong Yang (Mohnyin)
places.summary: A Tai state, also called Mong Yang.
places.notes: Present-day name as given in the AHOM catalogue.

places.name: Sankosh
places.location: Along the border of Assam and West Bengal, from Bhutan to the Brahmaputra system
places.summary: The river that divided Koch Bihar from Koch Hajo in 1581; roughly today's Assam-West Bengal border.

places.name: Bhareli
places.location: Arunachal Pradesh and Sonitpur district, Assam
places.summary: A north-bank river near Tezpur; the eastern limit of Koch Hajo, and where the 1663 treaty put the Ahom-Mughal frontier on the north bank (Samdhara on the Bharali).
places.notes: Spelled Bharali, Bhareli or Bhoroli in different sources.

places.name: Subansiri
places.location: Arunachal Pradesh and Assam (Lakhimpur and Dhemaji districts)
places.summary: A major north-bank river; the Chutia heartland lay on it, and Koch power briefly reached it under Nara Narayan.

places.name: Dibang
places.summary: An eastern river; the 'Dikshu' of the Kalika Purana is linked to it as the eastern limit of Kamarupa.
places.notes: Linking Dikshu to the Dibang rests on Sircar and Boruah.

places.name: Dikrang
places.location: Arunachal Pradesh and Lakhimpur district, Assam
places.summary: A north-bank river linked in tradition to the Dikkaravasini shrine on Kamarupa's eastern edge.
places.notes: The link rests on Dutta 2008; it is not the same as the 'Dikrai'.

places.name: Sisi
places.location: Upper Assam, north bank (exact reach approximate)
places.summary: Named as the western limit of the Chutia kingdom in one study.
places.notes: Present-day river approximate; not checked.

places.name: Lohit
places.summary: A great eastern tributary of the Brahmaputra; the Chutia valley lands lay between the Subansiri, Brahmaputra, Lohit and Dihing.

places.name: Parshuram Kund
places.summary: A sacred pool named as the eastern end of the Chutia holdings on the north bank.

places.name: Dhansiri
places.location: Golaghat and Dima Hasao districts, Assam, and Nagaland
places.summary: The valley of the early Dimasa (Kachari) kingdom; later a jungle buffer between the Kacharis and the Ahoms, and the limit of Ahom land in the 1520s-30s.

places.name: Asurar Ali
places.summary: A causeway (garh) at Guwahati; the south-bank mark of the 1639 Ahom-Mughal boundary.
places.notes: 'Believed to be' Rajgarh Road, Guwahati; the causeway survived into the late 1960s.

places.name: Kanchenjunga
places.summary: The mountain named as the northern limit of Kamarupa in the traditional description.

places.name: Mymensingh
places.summary: The southern limit of traditional Kamarupa, and later a southern part of Kamata (northern Mymensingh).

places.name: Ghoraghat
places.summary: A river crossing on the Karatoya; one study gives the southern edge of Biswa Singha's kingdom here.
places.notes: Location approximate.

places.name: Koch kingdom
places.summary: The kingdom founded by Biswa Singha in 1515; undivided under Nara Narayan until 1581.

places.name: Koch Hajo
places.summary: The eastern part of the divided Koch kingdom (1581 to 1613), north of the Brahmaputra between the Sankosh and the Bhareli.

places.name: Koch Bihar
places.summary: The western part of the divided Koch kingdom, west of the Sankosh.

places.name: Ahom kingdom
places.summary: The Tai-Ahom kingdom of 1228 to 1826.

places.name: Chutia kingdom
places.present_name: Far eastern Assam (Lakhimpur, Dhemaji, Tinsukia, Dibrugarh)
places.summary: The Sadiya-based kingdom annexed by the Ahoms in 1523-24.

places.name: Dimasa kingdom
places.summary: The Dimasa (Kachari) kingdom with capitals at Dimapur and later Maibong.

places.name: Bengal Sultanate
places.summary: The Sultanate of Gaur and Lakhnauti, which took Kamata in 1498.

places.name: Mughal Sarkar Kamrup
places.present_name: Western Assam between the Manas and Barnadi
places.summary: The Mughal administrative unit of Kamrup, later (1833-36) the basis of the British Kamrup district.
